client: I've been really dreading this networking event that's coming up next week for work. Every time I think about it, my heart starts racing and I get this sick feeling in my stomach — like I already know it's going to go badly. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the event is still going to happen whether I feel ready or not.
therapist: It sounds like this event is weighing on you heavily, and that physical anxiety response — the racing heart, the sick feeling — is your body already bracing for something it expects to be painful. I also notice you mentioned feeling unsure whether talking will even help, and I'm curious about that thought, because it sounds like part of you might feel a bit hopeless or stuck right now. What does "going badly" actually look like in your mind — what's the specific fear you keep coming back to?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess when I picture it going badly... I see myself trying to explain how I've been feeling, and my family just kind of glazing over, or worse, turning it into an argument about who's right. Like, there's this specific fear that I'll finally say something honest and vulnerable and my mom will just deflect it back to herself, or my brother will get defensive, and I'll end up feeling more alone than if I'd never said anything at all. That's the part that makes my chest tight — not just that it won't help, but that it might actually make things worse.
therapist: That fear of being more alone *after* opening up than before — that's such a painful and specific kind of dread, and it makes complete sense that it would sit in your chest like that. It sounds like part of you really *wants* to be heard by your family, otherwise the risk wouldn't feel so high. What would it mean to you if they *did* respond the way you're hoping — what would that give you that feels missing right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think if they actually listened... it would feel like I finally existed to them, like I wasn't just this background person they check in on out of obligation. There's this part of me that's been waiting for that my whole life, and saying it out loud like that makes me feel kind of embarrassed, like I'm asking for too much. But yeah, that's what's missing — just feeling like I actually matter to the people who are supposed to know me best.
therapist: What you just named — wanting to *matter* to the people who know you best — that's not asking for too much, that's one of the most fundamental human needs there is, and it's brave to say it out loud. I notice you moved through that pretty quickly, almost like you wanted to get past it before it could fully land, and I want to gently slow down here. Can we sit with that for a moment — what's it like to hear yourself say that you've been waiting for this your whole life?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: It's... uncomfortable, honestly, to just sit with it like that. Like if I let myself really feel how long I've been waiting, it starts to feel less like a want and more like something I've already failed at. I guess I moved past it quickly because staying there feels kind of hopeless, like I'm admitting that all this time I just haven't been enough for the people around me.
therapist: That thought — "I haven't been enough" — is such a heavy one to carry, and I want to gently name that it's flipping something important: the pain you're feeling comes from *other people* not showing up for you, but your mind is turning it into a verdict about *you*. That's such a common and cruel trick our minds play when we've been waiting a long time for something we needed. What do you think it would take to even begin questioning that verdict — the idea that their not seeing you means something was wrong with you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it... but it's hard not to take it personally when it's been a pattern across so many different people in my life. Like, if it was just one person who didn't see me, maybe I could chalk it up to them. But when it keeps happening over and over, it starts to feel like the common denominator is me. How do I argue with that kind of evidence?
therapist: That logic feels airtight when you're inside it, and I don't want to just dismiss it — but I want to offer a gentle reframe: a pattern of not being seen could also mean you've consistently been around people who *lacked the capacity* to see you, rather than that you're somehow unseeable. The way you just said that, so quietly and carefully, made me wonder if part of you is almost afraid to argue back against that belief — like hoping it's wrong might hurt more than just accepting it. What would it feel like to consider, even just as an experiment, that the pattern says something about what you've been *surrounded by*, rather than who you are?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That reframe is... I don't know, it's interesting, but it also feels a little too convenient, like something you'd say just to make me feel better. Because if I've just been surrounded by the wrong people my whole life, then that raises its own questions, like why do I keep ending up there, why do I keep choosing those situations. And honestly, yeah, you're right that there's something scary about hoping it's wrong, because I've let myself think that before and then just ended up back in the same place feeling even more foolish for having believed it.
therapist: That skepticism is actually really healthy — you're not just accepting a comfortable answer, you're stress-testing it, and that tells me you're thinking seriously rather than just looking for relief. The question you landed on, *why do I keep ending up in these situations*, is actually one of the most important ones we could explore, because it shifts from "what's wrong with me" to "what patterns have I learned," which is a very different and more workable question. Would you be open to gently looking at that — not as evidence against you, but as something that made sense given what you were taught to expect from people early on?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I mean... yeah, okay, I'm open to looking at it, but I'm already feeling a little defensive just hearing you frame it that way. Like, when you say "what I was taught to expect from people early on," I know where that's going, and part of me wants to say my childhood wasn't that bad, so maybe that's not even the right place to look. But I also can't ignore that this loneliness keeps showing up no matter who I'm around, so maybe there is something there I haven't fully faced.
therapist: That defensiveness you're noticing in yourself is actually really valuable information — it's worth paying attention to, not pushing past. And I want to honor what you said, because "it wasn't that bad" and "something shaped how I expect people to treat me" can both be true at the same time — it doesn't have to have been dramatic or terrible to have left a mark. What do you think it is about looking in that direction that feels like territory you'd rather not enter?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think part of it is that if I start picking apart how I learned to expect things from people, it starts to feel like I'm building a case against my family, and I really don't want to do that. They did their best, and I don't want to sit here and turn into someone who blames their parents for everything. It just feels like a road that leads somewhere I don't want to go.
therapist: The care you have for your family comes through so clearly, and wanting to protect them — and yourself — from feeling like this becomes a blame story makes a lot of sense. But I want to offer a gentle distinction: understanding how early relationships shaped what you learned to expect isn't the same as putting your family on trial — it's more like reading the instruction manual you were handed, so you can decide which parts still serve you. What if looking back wasn't about building a case against anyone, but about giving yourself some compassion for why certain patterns have felt so hard to break?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and the "instruction manual" thing is actually kind of a helpful way to put it. But I guess my worry is that once I start pulling on that thread, I won't be able to stop, and I'll just end up feeling worse about everything without any real resolution. It's like, what's the point of understanding where it all came from if I still have to go home and sit with the same loneliness at the end of the day?
therapist: That question — *what's the point of understanding if I still go home to the same loneliness* — is such an honest and important one, and I don't want to gloss over it with a tidy answer. You're right that insight alone doesn't fill an empty room, and part of what we'd be working toward isn't just understanding the pattern but slowly, carefully building something different — new expectations, new ways of recognizing and seeking out people who *can* show up for you. The thread doesn't have to unravel everything; it can also help you find where you want to start weaving something new.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's possible, but it feels really far away right now. Like, the idea of "weaving something new" sounds almost poetic, but when I think about actually doing it, I just picture myself putting myself out there and getting let down again. I've tried before and it hasn't really worked, so I guess I'm scared that this time won't be any different.
therapist: The fear of trying and being let down again — especially when you've already been there — is one of the most understandable reasons to hesitate, and I don't want to minimize how real that risk feels. What strikes me is that even as you're expressing doubt, you're still here, still engaging, still pushing back thoughtfully rather than shutting down — and that tells me something about you that the fear might be drowning out. What would it mean to you if this time *could* be even a little different — not perfect, but just different enough to matter?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
